newsitem.title: JAPAN: Lights dim for Japan's once-mighty coal industry.
newsitem.headline: Lights dim for Japan's once-mighty coal industry.

text.p: Japan will soon shut down its largest coal mine, signalling the demise of a once mighty domestic industry that in recent decades came to depend heavily on government subsidies for survival.
But the Japanese coal industry's loss will be a gain for coal exporters, especially Australia, as Japan's utilities turn increasingly to coal as an energy source, industry analysts say.
Mitsui Coal Mining Co Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Mitsui Mining Co Ltd, said this week it planned to close down the Miike Mine in Fukuoka Prefecture, southern Japan, at the end of March.
It said it had already started negotiating with labour unions on the terms of the closure, including retirement allowances to be paid to the mine's workers.

Only two other coal mines will remain in Japan, but they too will be no match for foreign coal once subsidies are halted, probably by March 2002, said Koji Morita, a senior economist with the Institute of Energy Economics (IEE).
The Miike mine, operated by Mitsui for over a century, produced about 6.5 million tonnes a year in its heyday in 1970.
In the late 1950s to early 1960s, Japan produced about 55 million tonnes of coal per year. Now annual domestic output is a mere six million tonnes.
Domestic coal's fortunes began to turn when relatively cheap supplies of crude oil began flooding in from the Middle East. It also came under attack from cheaper foreign coal.

Since 1963, when protective measures were adopted for the industry, administrative "guidance" from the government has compelled Japanese electric utilities to buy almost all domestic coal, at prices set by a government council, even though imported coal is much cheaper.

In 1994, domestic coal for electric utilities cost 16,650 yen ($135) per tonne compared with 4,330 yen ($35) per tonne of imported coal, government figures show. About 95 percent of Japan's annual coal consumption of 120 million tonnes is imported.
Production costs are steep for Japanese coal, which is mined much deeper than in Australia and many other countries.
While producers are cutting back, however, Japan's utilities are moving to boost coal use.

Coal will account for an estimated 15 percent of the energy supply at Japan's nine big electric utilities in 2005/2006, up from 10 percent in 1995/96, according to the Federation of Electric Power Companies, an industry body.
Australia, already the source of about 52 percent of Japan's coal imports in 1995, is expected to meet a large chunk of this increased demand, said IEE's Morita.
He said Australian coal was competitive because of its quality and massive reserves that could easily be mined.
Other countries such as Indonesia also had the potential to increase exports to Japan in the long run, he added.

Fuelling the switch to coal is government eagerness to reduce dependence on oil and a deep distrust of nuclear power among the public in Japan, aggravated by an accident at a prototype fast-breeder reactor in December 1995. This makes it hard for Japan's utilities to build new nuclear power plants. ($1=123 yen)
